categories.description: All questions from the Hawary source, shown as a separate view. They remain in their original chapters too.

facts.t: **Sudden (acute) dyspnoea** is caused by pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism and an attack of bronchial asthma, whereas **gradual progressive dyspnoea** is caused by COPD, interstitial pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and showers of pulmonary emboli; IPF never causes sudden dyspnoea, and pneumothorax never causes gradual dyspnoea.
**Acute dyspnoea with chest pain** suggests myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism or pneumothorax; an asthma attack causes dyspnoea with wheeze, but chest pain is not typical.

**Dyspnoea with wheeze** occurs in bronchial asthma, COPD and acute asthmatic bronchitis; **dyspnoea without wheeze** occurs in pleural effusion, pneumothorax, interstitial pulmonary fibrosis and primary emphysema.
**Orthopnoea** (dyspnoea on lying flat) occurs in left-sided heart failure, and also in bronchial asthma and interstitial pulmonary fibrosis.

A **localised fixed wheeze** means fixed local narrowing of a bronchus — an endobronchial tumour, an aspirated foreign body, or compression by an enlarged lymph node — whereas asthma gives generalised, variable wheeze.
Wheeze that **disappears with cough** is due to bronchial secretions; wheeze from bronchospasm or bronchial compression does not clear with cough.

**Dry cough** occurs in bronchial asthma, interstitial pulmonary fibrosis and pleurisy; **productive cough** occurs in pneumonia, bronchiectasis and lung abscess — bronchiectasis never gives a dry cough, and IPF never gives a productive cough.
**Rusty sputum** is characteristic of (lobar pneumococcal) pneumonia, and **copious purulent sputum** is characteristic of bronchiectasis.
Hazards and complications of **cough** include pneumothorax, hernia and cerebral haemorrhage; cough does not cause (transudative) pleural effusion.
**Pleuritic (pleural) chest pain** is stitching in character, increases with inspiration and cough, and decreases when the breath is held.
**Continuous agonising dull aching chest pain** is associated with bronchogenic carcinoma invading the chest wall or pleura, not with pleurisy or pulmonary embolism.

**Clubbing** is associated with bronchogenic carcinoma (lung cancer), bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease/IPF and cystic fibrosis; it is NOT associated with bronchial asthma, emphysema or uncomplicated COPD — clubbing in COPD should raise suspicion of carcinoma.
**Cyanosis** appears when reduced haemoglobin is at least **5 g/dL**.

**Central cyanosis** (including discoloration of the tongue) occurs in right-to-left shunt, marked polycythaemia and interstitial lung fibrosis, and does not improve on warming the hand; **peripheral cyanosis** is caused by shock, cold exposure and peripheral arterial disease, and improves on warming the hand.

**Bilateral congested non-pulsating neck veins** occur with obstruction of venous return — fibrosing mediastinitis, cardiac tamponade and superior vena cava thrombosis — but not as a non-metastatic (paraneoplastic) manifestation of oat-cell carcinoma.

**Superior vena cava obstruction** causes congested non-pulsating neck veins, morning facial oedema, and supraclavicular and suprasternal fullness, with dilated tortuous chest-wall veins that fill **from above downward** (in inferior vena cava obstruction they fill from below upward).

The **carina** (tracheal bifurcation) lies opposite the **sternal angle (angle of Louis/Lewis)**, which also lies opposite the aortic arch; the **transverse (horizontal) fissure** lies at the level of the **4th costal cartilage**.

**Barrel-shaped (hyperinflated, emphysematous) chest** is caused by hyperinflation in emphysema/COPD, with the anteroposterior diameter equal to the transverse diameter, horizontal ribs, dorsal kyphosis (not lordosis), a **wide subcostal angle** (not acute) and transverse shoulders.
**Kyphoscoliosis** causes an asymmetrical chest deformity, unlike symmetrical deformities such as barrel chest.

**Unilateral chest-wall retraction** is caused by volume loss — lung collapse, pulmonary fibrosis and pleural fibrosis (and kyphoscoliosis) — but not by lung consolidation, pleural effusion or pneumothorax, which do not reduce lung volume.
The **diaphragm** is the main muscle of ventilation; **abdominal paradox** (the abdomen moving inward during inspiration) is a sign of diaphragmatic paralysis.

**Indrawing of the intercostal spaces during inspiration** is a sign of increased airway resistance (strong negative intrathoracic pressure), not of intercostal muscle fatigue, diaphragmatic paralysis or pleurisy; prolonged expiration instead uses the abdominal muscles and pursed lips, and intercostal indrawing is a sign of difficult inspiration, not of prolonged expiration.
The **Litten sign** (the shadow of diaphragmatic excursion) is best seen in thin patients, not fatty ones, with the patient examined against light.
Chest **mobility is reduced** (never increased) by pleural effusion, bronchogenic carcinoma and pneumothorax.
**Tracheal tug** is detected in emphysema, where the hyperinflated chest pulls the trachea down on inspiration.

The **apex beat is shifted outside the midclavicular line** by right pleural effusion, right pneumothorax (pushing the mediastinum away) and right ventricular enlargement; right-sided collapse pulls the heart toward the right, so the apex lies near the left parasternal line.

**Tactile vocal fremitus (TVF) is increased** over pneumonic consolidation, a superficial cavity and a cavity surrounded by consolidation, because a patent bronchus conducts vibrations through solid lung; it is **decreased** over pneumothorax, pleural effusion, mesothelioma, emphysema, fibrosis and obstructive collapse (blocked bronchus), and a deep cavity does not increase it.

**Shifting dullness** over the chest occurs with **hydropneumothorax** (air plus fluid giving a level that shifts with posture, with diminished TVF and diminished breath sounds), not with free or encysted pleural effusion or encysted pneumothorax.

**Positive tidal percussion** (dullness moving with respiration) denotes **subdiaphragmatic** dullness, whereas **positive reversed tidal percussion** denotes diaphragmatic paralysis (paradoxical diaphragm movement).
**Unilateral hyperresonance** occurs with pneumothorax, giant bulla and compensatory emphysema; an attack of bronchial asthma causes bilateral, not unilateral, hyperresonance.

The **bare area of the heart** is normally **dull on light percussion** (it is not covered by lung); its dullness is increased by cardiomegaly, pericardial effusion and lingula collapse, and reduced by emphysema and hyperinflation overlapping the heart.

The **right border of the heart** is normally percussed **one finger to the right of the sternum**, and the **upper border of the liver** is detected by **heavy percussion at the right midclavicular line**.
**Traube's area** (normally tympanitic from the gastric bubble) becomes dull with left-sided pleural effusion, a full stomach or splenomegaly, but not with left lower lobe consolidation.
The boundaries of **Traube's area** include the tip of the left 8th costal cartilage (not the 6th), the left 9th rib and the left 11th rib in the mid-axillary line.

**Kronig's isthmus** is bounded by the **7th cervical spinous process** posteriorly (not T1), the sternoclavicular joint and the junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral third of the **clavicle** anteriorly, and the junction of the lateral two-thirds and medial third of the **scapular spine**; its lateral end is the line joining the clavicular and scapular-spine junctions, and the middle of the sternal notch is not a boundary.
A **dull Kronig's isthmus** may be due to a **superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumour**, not to emphysema or a consolidated anterior segment of the upper lobe.

**Vesicular breathing** is a gentle rustling sound with inspiration about **three times** expiration and **no gap** between inspiration and expiration; **bronchial breathing** is hollow, with inspiration **equal to** expiration and a **gap** between them.

**Bronchial breathing** is heard over consolidation, collapse with a patent bronchus, a superficial cavity with a patent bronchus and bronchopleural fistula, but not in bronchial asthma (diminished sounds with wheeze); **diminished breath sounds** occur with pleural effusion, pneumothorax and obstructive collapse, whereas pneumonia/consolidation gives bronchial breathing.

**Amphoric bronchial breathing** is a sign of a **superficial tense (tension) cavity** with a patent bronchus, not of pneumonic consolidation, a big cavity with a relaxed wall or encysted pneumothorax; **post-tussive suction** also occurs over a large cavity.

**Positive whispering pectoriloquy** occurs with **tubular bronchial breathing** (solid consolidation transmitting whispered speech), and is the characteristic feature of a **positive D'Espine sign**, which is due to **enlarged subcarinal (tracheobronchial) lymph nodes** transmitting voice sounds to the spines — not to a paratracheal mass, an enlarged left atrium or pericardial effusion.
**Late inspiratory crepitations** occur in interstitial pulmonary fibrosis; **bilateral basal crepitations with frothy sputum** indicate pulmonary oedema from left-sided heart failure.
A **pleural rub** is a to-and-fro sound whose intensity **increases** when the stethoscope is pressed against the chest wall, and which disappears when pleural effusion develops.
**Consolidation** shows **increased TVF, dullness on percussion and bronchial breathing**; a **superficial cavity** shows increased TVF and bronchial breathing but a **resonant** percussion note.

**Lung collapse** is caused by **total bronchial obstruction** (with absorption of air), pneumothorax or pleural effusion (compression), but not by partial bronchial obstruction, bronchospasm or interstitial pulmonary fibrosis; collapse shows **decreased TVF**.

**Obstructive collapse** shows diminished TVF, dullness and diminished breath sounds with the **trachea and mediastinum shifted toward the same side**; a **mass such as bronchogenic carcinoma** gives the same dull, diminished signs but pushes the trachea **to the opposite side**.

**Pleural effusion** shows **decreased TVF, stony dullness and diminished or absent breath sounds**, with the trachea shifted **away** from the affected side in massive effusion; **Skodaic resonance** and **aegophony** occur above its upper border, and shifting dullness is not a feature of free effusion.

**Simple pneumothorax** shows diminished TVF, hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds with a **central trachea**; **tension pneumothorax** shows the same signs with the trachea and mediastinum **shifted to the opposite side**.

systems.n: Obstructive Airway Disease: Asthma and COPD

facts.t: The main symptoms of **asthma** are **dyspnoea and wheeze** (not chest pain or haemoptysis); the **rapid reliever of bronchoconstriction** is a **β2-receptor agonist**, whereas sodium cromoglycate, nedocromil and antihistamines are not rapid relievers.

**Emphysema** is characterised by **progressive dyspnoea** with hyperinflation: **decreased TVF** over the apices, encroachment on the dullness of the bare area of the heart and on **hepatic dullness**, positive tracheal tug, and an absent apical pulsation.

In **COPD**, the neck veins show **expiratory filling** (raised intrathoracic pressure in expiration), and lung volumes show **increased residual volume, total lung capacity and functional residual capacity with decreased FVC**.

**Bronchiectasis** presents with chronic (years-long) cough and **copious purulent offensive sputum** that increases on leaning forward or postural change, with bilateral basal crepitations that **change with cough**; diagnosis is nowadays confirmed by **high-resolution CT (HRCT)**.

A **lung abscess** presents acutely with fever and cough for a few days followed by a **sudden gush of large amounts of purulent offensive sputum** (increasing when lying on the opposite side) as it ruptures into a bronchus, with bronchial breathing over the affected lobe.
**Suppurative lung syndromes** include lung abscess, bronchiectasis and infected lung cyst; **empyema** is a pleural collection, not a lung suppuration.

**Tuberculosis is transmitted mainly by droplet (airborne) infection**; food-borne (bovine milk) and intrauterine (congenital) spread also occur. In suspected pulmonary TB, the **contact history** must be stressed when taking the history.

Pulmonary TB radiology may show **cavitation, fibrosis and consolidation**; **active pulmonary TB is proved by positive sputum for acid-fast bacilli** — a positive tuberculin test, suggestive radiology or a raised ESR do not prove active disease.

A **positive tuberculin skin test** denotes **infection with or without disease** (not active disease only); it is read at **48–72 hours** and is positive when **induration (not erythema) exceeds 10 mm**.
**Rifampicin, pyrazinamide and isoniazid are hepatotoxic**, whereas **ethambutol is not** (its toxicity is optic neuritis); **rifampicin** causes **orange discoloration of body fluids**.

**Streptomycin** must be **totally avoided in pregnancy** (ototoxic to the fetus, affecting the 8th nerve) and avoided in **renal impairment** (nephrotoxic), whereas pyrazinamide can be used in renal impairment.
**Multidrug-resistant TB** organisms are mainly resistant to **isoniazid (INH) and rifampicin**.

systems.n: Tumours, Interstitial Lung Disease and Occupational Lung Disease

facts.t: **Asbestos exposure** is the main risk factor for **mesothelioma**.

**Bronchogenic (bronchial) carcinoma** may present with collapse, consolidation, effusion, lung abscess formation, or **normal physical findings**; **sputum cytology and chest X-ray** are the non-invasive tools used in screening for early lung cancer, whereas fibreoptic/rigid bronchoscopy and bronchography are invasive procedures.

**Interstitial pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)** presents with gradual progressive dyspnoea, a dry irritative cough, central cyanosis, clubbing and **bilateral diffuse late inspiratory crepitations**; **high-resolution CT (HRCT)** is the investigation of choice for interstitial lung diseases.
**Caplan syndrome** in coal workers' pneumoconiosis is associated with **rheumatoid arthritis**.

systems.n: Pulmonary Vascular Disease, Cor Pulmonale and Respiratory Failure

facts.t: **Pulmonary embolism** typically causes dyspnoea, chest pain and haemoptysis with **tachycardia — not bradycardia**; repeated showers of emboli can cause gradual progressive dyspnoea.
In **pulmonary hypertension** there is a **systolic murmur at the tricuspid area** and **dullness in the pulmonary area**; reversed splitting of the second heart sound is not a feature.

In **cor pulmonale**, palpable pulsations are felt in the **pulmonary area, epigastric area and left parasternal area** (right ventricular enlargement); the neck veins are **congested and pulsating**, with a **giant a wave** and systolic expansion, with tricuspid facies and a positive hepatojugular sign — but **pistol-shot sounds over the femoral artery** are a sign of aortic regurgitation, not cor pulmonale.
**Type II respiratory failure** is characterised by **hypoxaemia and hypercapnia** together (ventilatory failure), not by either alone.
Normal arterial blood gas values are **pH 7.35–7.45**, **PaCO2 35–45 mmHg** and **PaO2 80–100 mmHg**.
**Simple spirometry** can measure tidal volume, inspiratory capacity and expiratory reserve volume, but **cannot measure residual volume**.
In **restrictive lung disease**, vital capacity, residual volume and total lung capacity are all **reduced**, and spirometry shows **decreased FVC and FEV1 with a normal FEV1/FVC ratio**.

questions.q: Causes of acute (sudden) dyspnea include all the following except:
e: IPF causes gradual, progressive dyspnea, not sudden.

questions.q: Acute dyspnea with chest pain could be due to the following except:
e: Asthma causes dyspnea, wheeze and chest tightness — not true chest pain; myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism and pneumothorax all present with dyspnea plus chest pain.

questions.q: Gradual progressive dyspnea could be due to the following except:
e: Pneumothorax causes sudden dyspnea, not gradual.

questions.q: Causes of dyspnea with chest wheeze include the following:
e: Of these, only COPD causes wheeze; effusion and pneumothorax give dyspnea without wheeze.

questions.q: Causes of dyspnea with chest wheeze include the following except:
e: IPF causes dyspnea with dry cough and fine end-inspiratory crackles, not wheeze; asthma, COPD and acute asthmatic bronchitis narrow the airways and wheeze.

questions.q: Orthopnea occurs in:
f: Answer key corrected to A (the duplicate copy lists D).
e: Lying flat increases venous return and raises the diaphragm, worsening pulmonary congestion — orthopnea of left heart failure, relieved by sitting up; asthma and IPF dyspnea is not positional in this way.

questions.q: Dry cough could be due to the following except:
e: Bronchiectasis gives a productive cough with copious purulent sputum.

questions.q: Productive cough could be due to the following except:
e: IPF causes a dry cough with gradual dyspnea and fine end-inspiratory crackles; pneumonia, bronchiectasis and lung abscess all produce productive, purulent sputum.

questions.q: Hazards of cough include the following except:
e: Cough does not cause transudative effusion.

questions.q: Rusty sputum is characteristic of:
e: Rusty sputum is typical of lobar (pneumococcal) pneumonia.

questions.q: Purulent sputum is characteristic of:
e: Bronchiectasis produces copious purulent sputum.

questions.q: Localized fixed wheeze could be due to:
e: A fixed localized wheeze means a local bronchial narrowing, e.g. an endobronchial tumor.

questions.q: Localized fixed wheeze could be due to the following except:
o: Compression of a bronchus by enlarged lymph node
e: Asthma gives generalized, variable wheeze, not a fixed localized one.

questions.q: Chest wheezes that disappear with cough could be due to:
e: Wheeze from secretions clears with cough; bronchospasm or compression does not.

questions.q: Chest pain of pleural origin is characterized by the following except:
e: Pleural pain is worsened by deep breathing and cough, and eased by holding the breath.

questions.q: Stitching chest pain that increases with inspiration and decreases with holding breath could be due to:
e: Pleuritic pain eases when the breath is held, as the inflamed layers stop rubbing.

questions.q: Continuous agonizing dull aching chest pain is associated with:
e: Chest wall/pleural invasion by carcinoma gives constant, severe, dull aching pain.

questions.q: Dyspnea without chest wheeze could be due to:
e: Effusion, emphysema and IPF all cause dyspnea without wheeze.

questions.q: (p.30) Complications of chronic cough include all except:
e: Pleural effusion is not a complication of chronic cough.

questions.q: Bilateral congested non-pulsating neck veins occur in all the following EXCEPT:
o: Extra-pulmonary non-metastatic manifestations of oat cell carcinoma
e: Paraneoplastic (non-metastatic) manifestations do not obstruct venous return; the others do.

questions.q: Clubbing of fingers is associated with the following EXCEPT:
e: Bronchial asthma is not associated with clubbing.

questions.q: Clubbing is present in all EXCEPT:
e: Emphysema/COPD does not cause clubbing; if present, suspect carcinoma.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT associated with clubbing of fingers?
e: COPD does not cause clubbing; finger clubbing in a COPD patient warrants investigation for lung cancer, bronchiectasis or fibrosis.

questions.q: Warming the hand in peripheral cyanosis:
e: Warming improves circulation, so peripheral cyanosis improves; central (tongue) cyanosis does not.

questions.q: Warming the hand in central cyanosis:
e: Central cyanosis comes from desaturated arterial blood, so warming cannot correct it: increased local flow and oxygen extraction make the hand look more cyanosed, unlike peripheral cyanosis, which improves with warming. The tongue stays blue because it reflects arterial saturation.

questions.q: Causes of peripheral cyanosis include all of the following except:
e: Right-to-left shunt causes central cyanosis.

questions.q: In cyanosis the reduced hemoglobin should not be less than:
e: Cyanosis appears when reduced hemoglobin is 5 g/dl or more.

questions.q: Central cyanosis occurs in all of the following except:
e: Shock causes peripheral (low-flow) cyanosis, not central.

questions.q: In cyanosis the reduced hemoglobin should not be less than:
e: Central cyanosis appears when reduced Hb is at least 5 g/dl.

questions.q: Bifurcation of the trachea (carina) lies opposite:
o: Below the bifurcation of the pulmonary conus
e: The carina lies at the level of the sternal angle (angle of Louis).

questions.q: Angle of Lewis is opposite the following except:
e: The sternal angle lies opposite the aortic arch and the carina, not a bronchial stump.

questions.q: The transverse fissure is present at the level of:
e: The transverse fissure lies at the level of the 4th costal cartilage.

questions.q: Barrel shaped chest is caused by:
e: Barrel chest results from chronic hyperinflation with an increased anteroposterior diameter, loss of elastic recoil and air trapping, classically in emphysema / COPD (the 'emphysematous' chest).

questions.q: Barrel shaped chest is characterized by the following except:
o: The anteroposterior diameter equals the transverse diameter
e: Barrel chest has dorsal kyphosis, not lordosis.

questions.q: Regarding hyperinflation (barrel chest), all of the following are true except:
e: In hyperinflation the ribs become horizontal, not oblique.

questions.q: Symmetrical abnormal chest shape EXCEPT:
e: Barrel chest, pectus carinatum and pectus excavatum deform the chest symmetrically; kyphoscoliosis twists the spine and rib cage, so the deformity is asymmetrical — it is the exception.

questions.q: Unilateral chest wall retraction could be due to:
e: Collapse reduces lung volume, so the chest wall retracts on that side.

questions.q: Unilateral chest retraction occurs with the following except:
e: Consolidation does not reduce lung volume, so there is no retraction.

questions.q: The main muscle of ventilation is:
e: The diaphragm is the main muscle of ventilation.

questions.q: Abdominal paradox is a sign of:
e: In diaphragmatic paralysis the diaphragm cannot descend, so inspiratory negative pressure sucks it upward and the abdomen moves inward during inspiration while the rib cage expands — abdominal paradox, a form of paradoxical thoraco-abdominal movement.

questions.q: Indrawing of the intercostal spaces during inspiration is a sign of:
e: Indrawing reflects strong negative pressure against raised airway resistance.

questions.q: All of the following occur in prolonged expiration except:
e: Indrawing is a sign of difficult inspiration, not of prolonged expiration.

questions.q: One of the following increases the mobility of the chest:
e: Effusion, carcinoma and pneumothorax all reduce chest movement.

questions.q: About Litten sign, the following is right except:
o: Should be detected with patient against sunlight
e: Litten sign is best seen in thin patients, not fatty ones.

questions.q: Presence of dilated tortuous veins over the chest wall which fill from above downward is due to:
e: Collateral veins fill downward when the SVC is obstructed.

questions.q: Tracheal tug could be detected in:
e: Hyperinflated chest in emphysema pulls the trachea down with inspiration.

questions.q: What shifts the apex outside the midclavicular line?
e: Effusion or pneumothorax pushes the mediastinum, and RV enlargement shifts the apex outward.

questions.q: Causes of apex at the left parasternal line:
e: Right collapse pulls the heart to the right, so the apex lies near the left parasternal line.

questions.q: Causes of palpable pulsation over the chest wall:
questions.sa: Epigastric & left parasternal pulsations (RV enlargement, e.g. cor pulmonale); apical pulsation absent in emphysema
e: A palpable pulsation is usually a hyperdynamic or enlarged right ventricle felt at the epigastrium and left parasternal area, e.g. in cor pulmonale. In emphysema the hyperinflated lung covers the heart, so the apical pulsation is absent.

questions.q: T.V.F. is usually increased over:
e: Solid consolidation conducts vibrations well, so TVF rises.

questions.q: Increased TVF occurs in all of the following except:
o: Cavity surrounded by an area of consolidation
e: Obstructive collapse has a blocked bronchus, so TVF is decreased.

questions.q: TVF is increased in the following except:
e: A deep cavity does not increase TVF; a superficial cavity with a patent bronchus does.

questions.q: TVF is decreased in the following conditions except:
e: A superficial cavity increases TVF.

questions.q: All the following show reduced T.V.F. except:
e: Consolidation increases TVF.

questions.q: Unilateral chest wall retraction could be due to the following except:
e: Consolidation does not reduce lung volume, so no retraction. Collapse and fibrosis shrink the lung.

questions.q: TVF is increased in the following condition:
e: Cavity with patent bronchus conducts vibrations better. The others decrease TVF.

questions.q: Shifting dullness over the chest occurs with:
e: Air and fluid together give a level that shifts with posture (hydropneumothorax).

questions.q: Presence of positive tidal percussion denotes that the dullness is due to:
e: On deep inspiration the diaphragm descends, carrying the upper border of subdiaphragmatic dullness (liver, spleen) downward — this respiratory movement of the dullness border is tidal percussion.

questions.q: Presence of positive reversed tidal percussion could be due to:
e: In diaphragmatic paralysis the affected hemidiaphragm moves paradoxically upward on inspiration, so the dullness border moves in the reverse direction — reversed tidal percussion.

questions.q: The bare area of the heart is normally:
e: The bare area is not covered by lung, so it is dull on light percussion.

questions.q: The dullness of the bare area of the heart is increased in the following conditions except:
e: Emphysema hyperinflates the lungs, which overlap the heart and shrink the bare area; cardiomegaly and pericardial effusion enlarge the cardiac silhouette, and collapse of the lingula uncovers more of the heart — all three increase the dullness.

questions.q: The dullness of the bare area of the heart is increased in case of:
e: Cardiomegaly enlarges the heart, so more of it lies uncovered by lung and the bare-area dullness increases. Emphysema and asthma hyperinflate the lungs, which overlap the heart and reduce the dullness instead.

questions.q: Clinically, the right border of the heart can be percussed normally at:
o: One finger to the right of the sternum
One cm to the right of the lower half of the sternum
One cm to the right of mid-sternal line at lower half of the sternum
e: The right border (formed by the right atrium) is percussed immediately to the right of the sternum — about one finger breadth from its edge. That bedside surface marking is the taught landmark.

questions.q: Dullness of Traube’s area is due to the following except:
e: Lung consolidation does not fill Traube’s area; effusion, full stomach and splenomegaly do.

questions.q: Traube’s dullness occurs with:
e: A left pleural effusion fills the pleural space over the stomach fundus and replaces the normal tympanic resonance of Traube’ area with dullness; consolidation or collapse of the left lower lobe does not occupy this space.

questions.q: Boundaries of Traube’s area include the following except:
f: Answer key follows the source bank; textbook descriptions of Traube's upper boundary vary - verify.
e: Traube's (semilunar) space is the tympanic gastric area bounded by the left costal margin below (8th cartilage) and the 9th and 11th ribs in the mid-axillary line laterally; the tip of the 6th costal cartilage is not one of its named boundaries in this bank's account. Note: this is the original bank's answer; textbook descriptions of the upper boundary vary.

questions.q: Dull Kronig’s isthmus may be due to:
o: Consolidated anterior segment of upper lobe
e: A superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumor makes Kronig’s isthmus dull.

questions.q: Unilateral hyperresonance occurs with the following except:
e: An asthma attack causes bilateral, not unilateral, hyperresonance.

questions.q: The upper border of the liver can be detected by:
o: Heavy percussion at the right midclavicular line
Light percussion at the right midclavicular line
e: Heavy percussion reaches the liver’s upper border beneath the lung.

questions.q: Kronig’s isthmus boundaries include the following except:
o: Junction between the lateral third and medial two thirds of the clavicle
Junction between the lateral two thirds and medial third of the scapular spine
e: The isthmus lies over the shoulder between the clavicle and the scapular spine, not at the sternal notch.

questions.q: Boundaries of Kronig’s isthmus, all except:
o: Junction between medial 2/3 and lateral 1/3 of the clavicle
e: The posterior boundary is the C7 spinous process, not T1.

questions.q: Lateral end of Kronig’s isthmus is:
o: Contact of acromion process with clavicle
Line of contact between junction of medial two thirds & lateral one third of clavicle and junction of lateral two thirds & medial one third of scapular spine
e: Kronig's isthmus is the band of resonance over the lung apex; its lateral end is the line joining the junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third of the clavicle to the junction of the lateral two-thirds and medial one-third of the scapular spine.

questions.q: The following conditions are associated with diminished breath sounds except:
e: Consolidation usually gives bronchial breathing, not diminished breath sounds.

questions.q: The following is associated with diminished intensity of breath sounds:
e: Effusion, collapse and pneumothorax all diminish breath sound intensity.

questions.q: In auscultation, vesicular breathing is characterized by the following except:
o: Inspiration is three times the expiration
No gap between inspiration and expiration
e: Vesicular: inspiration longer than expiration with no gap; equal inspiration/expiration is bronchial.

questions.q: In auscultation, bronchial breathing is characterized by the following except:
o: Inspiration is three times the expiration
e: Bronchial: inspiration equals expiration with a gap; 3:1 is vesicular.

questions.q: Bronchial breathing can be heard above:
e: Consolidation transmits bronchial breathing from a patent bronchus.

questions.q: Bronchial breathing is found in all the following except:
e: Asthma has narrowed airways, so breath sounds are diminished with wheeze, not bronchial.

questions.q: Amphoric breathing is a sign of presence of:
e: Amphoric breathing indicates a tense cavity with a patent bronchus.

questions.q: Amphoric bronchial breathing occurs with:
e: A superficial tense cavity with a patent bronchus gives high-pitched, metallic amphoric breathing; a large cavity with a relaxed wall gives low-pitched cavernous breathing instead.

questions.q: Presence of positive D’Espine sign could be due to:
e: Enlarged subcarinal nodes transmit the voice to the spine (D’Espine sign).

questions.q: Positive D’Espine sign is characterized by:
e: D’Espine sign is a positive whispering pectoriloquy over the spines.

questions.q: Late inspiratory crepitations occur with:
e: Fibrosis gives fine end-inspiratory (velcro-like) crepitations that do not clear after coughing — the classic auscultatory sign of IPF.

questions.q: Positive whispering pectoriloquy occurs with:
e: Tubular breathing (solid consolidation) transmits whispered speech clearly.

questions.q: Post-tussive suction occurs with:
e: After a cough empties a large cavity, air rushes back in through the patent bronchus and produces a suction sound over the cavity.

questions.q: Pleural rub is characterized by all except:
o: It is a to & fro sound
Intensity increases by pressing the stethoscope against chest wall
Intensity decreases by pressing the stethoscope against chest wall
Disappears upon occurrence of pleural effusion
e: Pressing the stethoscope brings the roughened pleural surfaces together, so the rub gets louder, not quieter; it disappears when pleural effusion separates the surfaces.

questions.q: A case with an area of increased TVF, resonant percussion note and bronchial breathing on auscultation. These are the physical findings of:
e: A superficial cavity is an air-filled space with a patent bronchus: it conducts vibrations and tubular sounds well (increased TVF, bronchial breathing) but, being air-filled, stays resonant — unlike solid consolidation, which is dull.

questions.q: A case with increased TVF, bronchial breathing and dullness on percussion. The diagnosis is:
e: Solid, airless lung conducts sound better than aerated lung (increased TVF, bronchial breathing) and percusses dull. Effusion and pneumothorax both decrease TVF, so they are excluded.

questions.q: Collapse is characterized by:
e: In obstructive collapse the bronchus is blocked, so vibrations and breath sounds cannot be conducted to the chest wall — TVF falls. Consolidation does the opposite (increased TVF) because the bronchus stays patent through solid lung.

questions.q: The following condition leads to lung collapse:
e: Total obstruction traps distal air, which is absorbed into the blood, so the segment collapses. Partial obstruction instead acts as a ball valve and causes localized emphysema, not collapse.

questions.q: All of the following cause lung collapse EXCEPT:
e: Pneumothorax and effusion collapse lung by compression, and complete obstruction by air absorption. Partial obstruction lets air in but traps it (ball-valve effect), causing localized emphysema instead of collapse.

questions.q: A case with decreased TVF, dullness and diminished breath sounds over the left hemithorax with shift of the trachea to the left. These are the physical findings of:
e: Volume loss pulls the trachea toward the affected side, while the airless collapsed lung gives dullness with decreased TVF and diminished sounds. Effusion and pneumothorax push the trachea away, and consolidation increases TVF without shift.

questions.q: A short case about a patient complaining of dyspnea, diminished air entry on the left side and mediastinal shift to the left side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e: A shift toward the diseased side means volume loss — collapse. Pneumothorax and effusion occupy space and push the mediastinum to the opposite side.

questions.q: A case with diminished TVF, dullness and diminished breath sounds over the right clavicular and infraclavicular regions with shift of the trachea to the right side. These are the physical signs of:
e: The trachea is pulled toward the side of volume loss, and the collapsed lobe gives dullness with decreased TVF and diminished sounds. Consolidation would increase TVF, and a bulla would be hyper-resonant.

questions.q: A case with diminished TVF, dullness and diminished breath sounds over the right clavicular and infraclavicular regions with shift of the trachea to the LEFT side. These are the physical findings of:
e: A push to the opposite side means a space-occupying mass, not volume loss: carcinoma is the only mass among the options. Collapse would pull the trachea to the same side, and consolidation causes no shift.

questions.q: Bilateral basal crepitations with frothy sputum. The most likely diagnosis is:
e: Left heart failure floods the alveoli: fluid crackles at the bases and produces frothy (pink-tinged) sputum. Asthma instead gives wheeze with prolonged expiration.

questions.q: A case with area of increased TVF, dullness and bronchial breathing. These are physical findings of:
e: Solid lung conducts sound (increased TVF, bronchial breathing) and percusses dull — the consolidation triad. Collapse decreases TVF, pneumothorax is hyper-resonant with decreased TVF, and an abscess gives cavity signs.

questions.q: Normal pH of arterial blood (ABG) is:
e: Normal arterial pH is 7.35–7.45; below 7.35 is acidaemia and above 7.45 is alkalaemia.

questions.q: Normal PCO2 in arterial blood is:
e: Normal PaCO2 is 35-45 mmHg.

questions.q: Normal oxygen tension (PaO2) in arterial blood gases is:
e: Normal PaO2 on room air is 80–100 mmHg. It is the key ABG measure of oxygenation and falls with age; it is distinct from oxygen saturation (SaO2).

questions.q: Simple spirometry can measure all of the following EXCEPT:
e: Spirometry measures only air that can be breathed in or out, so residual volume — the air left in the lungs after maximal expiration — cannot be measured by it; lung volumes need helium dilution or body plethysmography.

questions.q: In restrictive lung disease, the following volumes are reduced:
e: Restriction shrinks the lung, so all volumes fall: VC, RV and TLC are all reduced (book Table 3-9) — the opposite of obstruction, where air trapping raises RV and TLC.

questions.q: A patient with decreased FVC and FEV1 but a normal FEV1/FVC ratio is suggested to have:
e: A preserved FEV1/FVC ratio excludes airflow obstruction (obstruction = ratio <70%); when FVC and FEV1 both fall with a normal ratio, the pattern is restrictive — small lungs, not narrowed airways.

questions.q: Main symptom in asthma is:
e: Asthma presents mainly with dyspnea and wheeze.

questions.q: Rapid reliever of bronchoconstriction is:
e: Beta-2 agonists are rapid relievers; cromoglycate and nedocromil are preventers.

questions.q: Emphysema is characterized by:
e: Progressive, persistent dyspnea is the cardinal symptom of emphysema/COPD; hemoptysis is not a feature and needs work-up for lung cancer.

questions.q: Emphysema is characterized by all except:
questions.sa: Acute subcostal angle (the subcostal angle is wide in emphysema)
e: Emphysema causes hyperinflation with a wide (obtuse) subcostal angle, barrel chest and diminished breath sounds; an acute (narrow) subcostal angle is the normal finding, so it is the exception.

questions.q: Neck veins in COPD:
e: Raised intrathoracic pressure fills the neck veins in expiration in COPD.

questions.q: Emphysema may be accompanied by all the following except:
o: Encroachment on dullness of the bare area of the heart
e: TVF is decreased, not increased, over emphysematous apices.

questions.q: In emphysema:
o: Bare area of heart becomes widened
e: Hyperinflated lungs encroach on hepatic dullness.

questions.q: In COPD all increases except:
e: In COPD FVC falls while RV, TLC and FRC rise.

questions.q: A case with cough and expectoration of large amount of purulent offensive sputum for 10 years which increases on leaning forward. The examination revealed bilateral basal crepitations which change with cough. The possible diagnosis is:
e: A 10-year history of copious fetid sputum that increases with posture, with coarse basal crackles that change after coughing, is bronchiectasis: permanently dilated airways pool secretions that drain posturally. A lung abscess is acute (days) and presents with fever and a sudden gush of foul sputum.

questions.q: Diagnosis of bronchiectasis is confirmed nowadays by:
e: HRCT chest is the investigation of choice — it directly shows airway dilatation and wall thickening, while a chest X-ray may be normal.

questions.q: A case with history of fever and cough for few days followed by sudden gush of large amount of purulent offensive sputum which increases on lying on the left side. The examination revealed bronchial breathing over the right infra-scapular region. The possible diagnosis is:
e: A sudden gush after fever suggests a lung abscess rupturing into a bronchus, here right lower lobe.

questions.q: Suppurative lung syndromes include the following except:
e: Empyema is a pleural collection, not a lung suppuration.

questions.q: A case with history of fever and cough for a few days followed by sudden gush of a large amount of purulent offensive sputum which increases on lying on the left side. The examination revealed bronchial breathing over the right infrascapular region. The possible diagnosis is:
e: Acute onset, sudden rupture into a bronchus; sputum rises when lying on the opposite side; signs are on the right lower zone.

questions.q: Tuberculosis is transmitted by:
f: Answer key corrected to D (the PDF key lists A).
e: Airborne droplets from an active pulmonary case are the main route, after prolonged exposure — especially with cavitary disease. Bovine (unpasteurized-milk) and congenital spread are rare but recognized, hence 'all of the above'.

questions.q: Taking history in a case suspected to be pulmonary T.B. should stress upon:
e: TB needs prolonged close exposure to an infectious case, so a history of contact with active pulmonary TB is the highest-yield item — more discriminating than routine present, past, or family history.

questions.q: The radiological finding in pulmonary tuberculosis is:
e: Post-primary TB classically cavitates at the apices/upper zones, heals by fibrosis and calcification, and can present with consolidation — so all three patterns occur. Upper-zone patchy/nodular shadows are the classic CXR picture.

questions.q: The diagnosis of active pulmonary tuberculosis is proved by:
o: Positive sputum for acid fast bacilli
e: Demonstrating acid-fast bacilli in sputum proves active disease. A positive tuberculin test only shows exposure/infection and cannot confirm active TB, while CXR shadows and raised ESR are non-specific. (Culture is the gold standard, but it is not among the options.)

questions.q: Positive tuberculin test denotes:
e: A positive test measures delayed-type hypersensitivity: it supports exposure/infection but cannot confirm active disease. Conversely, a negative test does not rule out active TB — false negatives reach 30–50% in severe or immunocompromised disease.

questions.q: The tuberculin skin test is read after:
e: The tuberculin test is read 48–72 hours after injection.

questions.q: The tuberculin skin test is considered positive if:
e: Induration (not erythema) is measured; more than 10 mm is positive.

questions.q: The following anti-tuberculous drugs have hepatotoxic effect except:
e: Ethambutol is not hepatotoxic (its toxicity is optic neuritis).

questions.q: The anti-tuberculous drug that leads to orange discoloration of body fluids is:
e: Rifampicin stains body secretions orange-red — urine, sweat, tears and sputum — a harmless effect patients must be warned about so they do not mistake it for bleeding. None of the other first-line drugs does this.

questions.q: The following anti-TB drugs can be used safely in renal impairment except:
e: Streptomycin needs a major dose reduction in renal failure and carries irreversible vestibular and auditory toxicity, so it is the exception. Pyrazinamide remains usable.

questions.q: Which of the anti-TB drugs should be totally avoided in pregnancy?
e: Streptomycin causes irreversible vestibular and auditory (8th-nerve) damage and must be avoided in pregnancy for fetal ototoxicity. Isoniazid, rifampicin and ethambutol are considered safe in pregnancy.

questions.q: Organisms resistant to T.B drugs are mainly resistant to:
e: Multidrug-resistant TB is resistant to INH and rifampicin.

questions.q: Exposure to asbestos is the main risk factor for:
e: Asbestos is the classic risk factor for malignant pleural mesothelioma, which typically causes a rapid, massive haemorrhagic pleural effusion. Smoking — not asbestos — is the dominant factor for bronchogenic carcinoma.

questions.q: Bronchogenic carcinoma can be presented by:
e: A tumor may be asymptomatic, obstruct a bronchus so the distal lung collapses and becomes infected (recurrent, resistant pneumonia/consolidation), or break down into a lung abscess — so all three presentations occur.

questions.q: Screening for detection of early lung cancer includes:
e: Of the listed options, only sputum cytology and chest X-ray are non-invasive; bronchoscopy and bronchography are invasive diagnostic procedures, not screening tests. Note: the department book does not cover lung-cancer screening at all — its workup is CXR/HRCT plus bronchoscopy and biopsy for diagnosis.

questions.q: Bronchial carcinoma may present with:
e: Complete bronchial obstruction collapses the distal lung; infection in the collapsed segment causes recurrent pneumonia (consolidation); direct pleural invasion causes a haemorrhagic, rapidly accumulating effusion.

questions.q: A case with history of gradual progressive dyspnea and dry irritative cough. The general examination revealed central cyanosis and third degree clubbing of fingers. The local examination revealed bilateral diffuse late inspiratory crepitations. The possible diagnosis is:
e: Gradual progressive dyspnea with dry cough, cyanosis, clubbing and end-inspiratory leathery crepitations that do not clear with coughing are the classic ILD/IPF picture. Bronchiectasis gives purulent sputum with coarse crackles, and heart failure gives basal crepitations with edema and frothy sputum.

questions.q: What is the investigation of choice for diagnosis of interstitial lung diseases?
e: HRCT detects early ILD and shows its extent, type and activity: honeycombing is the hallmark of IPF and essential for a definite diagnosis, while ground-glass change indicates inflammation and a reticular pattern indicates fibrosis.

questions.q: Caplan syndrome in coal worker’s pneumoconiosis is associated with:
e: Caplan syndrome is pneumoconiosis with rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.q: The palpable pulsations in a case of cor pulmonale are felt in:
e: RV enlargement gives pulsation in the pulmonary, epigastric and left parasternal areas.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical clinical finding in pulmonary embolism?
e: PE causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.

questions.q: Neck veins in cor pulmonale show:
e: Raised right atrial pressure congests the neck veins; forceful atrial contraction against a stiff, hypertensive right ventricle produces a giant a wave, and functional tricuspid regurgitation produces systolic expansion of the veins.

questions.q: Cor pulmonale shows the following except:
o: Pistol shot over the femoral artery
e: Pistol shot femoral is a sign of aortic regurgitation, not cor pulmonale.

questions.q: In pulmonary hypertension, there may be:
o: Wide splitting of the 2nd heart sound
Dullness in the 2nd right intercostal space
e: In pulmonary hypertension P2 is loud and the split is usually narrow, because high pulmonary pressure closes the pulmonary valve early; wide splitting can still occur when right ventricular ejection is prolonged (e.g., right bundle branch block, an ECG finding in PH), so it 'may' be found. Dullness in the 2nd right space is an aortic-area sign, and tricuspid regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension is functional (annular dilatation), not organic.

questions.q: In pulmonary hypertension, all are true except:
o: Wide splitting of 2nd heart sound at pulmonary area
Reversed splitting of 2nd heart sound at pulmonary area
e: Reversed (paradoxical) splitting means the aortic valve closes after the pulmonary valve — a left-sided phenomenon (left bundle branch block, severe aortic stenosis), not a feature of pulmonary hypertension. Wide splitting, a tricuspid systolic murmur from functional regurgitation, and dullness in the pulmonary area can all occur in PH.

questions.q: During physical examination of a patient with suspected left sided pleural effusion, which combination of physical signs is classic for a fluid-filled pleural space?
o: Increased TVF, stony dull percussion, bronchial breathing
Decreased tactile vocal fremitus, stony dull percussion, absent/diminished breath sounds
Normal tactile vocal fremitus, tympanitic percussion, vesicular breathing with wheezes
Increased tactile vocal fremitus, dull percussion, amphoric breathing
e: Fluid separates the lung from the chest wall: it damps vibration (decreased TVF) and breath sounds and percusses stony dull. Increased TVF with bronchial breathing would mean consolidation, not fluid.

questions.q: Main finding in pleural effusion is:
o: Stony dullness with diminished breath sounds
e: Stony dullness with diminished breath sounds is the hallmark: fluid is dull to percussion and blocks sound transmission. Dullness with increased TVF or increased breath sounds points to consolidation instead.

questions.q: Low TVF, dullness, diminished breath sounds on the left side and shift of the trachea to the right. Diagnosis?
e: Fluid abolishes vibration and breath sounds and gives stony dullness; a large left effusion also pushes the trachea and mediastinum to the opposite (right) side. Consolidation would increase TVF with bronchial breathing and no shift.

questions.q: Pleural effusion is accompanied by the following physical signs except:
o: Skodaic resonance above its upper border
e: Skodaic resonance and aegophony occur above the upper border of an effusion, over compressed lung. A shifting fluid level belongs to hydropneumothorax — air plus fluid in the pleural space — not to a simple effusion.

questions.q: A case with diminished TVF, hyper-resonance and diminished breath sounds over the left hemithorax with shift of the trachea to the right side. These are physical findings of:
e: Air in the pleural space gives hyper-resonance with decreased fremitus and breath sounds; under tension, rising pressure pushes the trachea to the opposite side and causes hypotension and cyanosis — an emergency. Effusion would be dull, and consolidation increases TVF.

questions.q: A case with diminished TVF, hyper-resonance and diminished breath sounds over the left hemithorax and the trachea is central. These are physical findings of:
e: Hyper-resonance with decreased fremitus and breath sounds means air in the pleural space; a central trachea excludes tension, which would push it to the opposite side. Effusion would percuss dull, not hyper-resonant.

questions.q: A case with diminished TVF, positive shifting dullness and diminished breath sounds over the left hemithorax. These are physical findings of:
e: Hydropneumothorax holds both air and fluid: the fluid level shifts with posture (shifting dullness), while air and fluid together diminish fremitus and breath sounds. Pure pneumothorax has no fluid level and pure effusion has no air.

questions.q: Tension pneumothorax shows the following clinical signs except:
o: Shift of mediastinum to opposite side
e: Cavernous breathing is not a sign of tension pneumothorax; amphoric is.

questions.q: Type II respiratory failure is characterized by:
e: Type II (hypercapnic) respiratory failure is PaO2 <60 mmHg with PaCO2 >45 mmHg, caused by alveolar hypoventilation; type I is hypoxemia with a normal or low PaCO2.

questions.q: Superior vena cava obstruction is characterized by the following except:
o: Dilated veins over the chest wall which fill from down upward
e: In SVC obstruction chest wall veins fill from above downward.
